content.text: The text surveys the classification and development of Romanesque, Byzantine, Lombardic, and Gothic architecture. It argues that “Romanesque” should broadly encompass transitional Western styles, while “Byzantine” properly denotes Eastern Christian architecture. Byzantine architecture evolved from basilicas to domed churches, culminating in Justinian’s Hagia Sophia, then declined into Neo-Byzantine forms that influenced Armenia and Russia. Armenia transmitted Byzantine and Sassanian traditions northward; Russian architecture remained largely derivative, adopting Tartar bulbous domes. Italian architecture combined Roman, Byzantine, Lombardic, and Gothic influences: northern Italy developed vaulted, round-arched Lombardic churches, while central and southern regions retained Byzantine-Romanesque forms. Later Italian Gothic adopted pointed arches but generally lacked Northern Gothic structural and vertical principles. Important examples include Bethlehem, Thessalonica, Ravenna, Venice, Pisa, Milan, Florence, and numerous Armenian and Russian churches. Princess Olga was baptized at Constantinople; the Normans entered and conquered parts of Italy and Sicily.
